I completely understand why this feels overwhelming — and **please know it's absolutely okay to prioritize your family's financial stability**. Community celebrations are about *togetherness*, not about one family carrying the entire burden. Here’s how to navigate this thoughtfully and compassionately: --- ### ✨ **Key Truths to Remember:** - **"Enough for the whole community" is almost never literal** — no single family is expected to feed hundreds of people. This is likely a misunderstanding or an outdated expectation. - **True community spirit is about shared effort** — not one family doing all the work while others contribute nothing. - **Your family’s well-being comes first**. He said our oldest sister is going to be pissed and i have to tell her myself. He wished me luck. So I call her and she is mad. She says she’ll probably have to end up hosting even though she is up next for Christmas and I’m being inconsiderate of what our mom asked us to do. “Mom wouldn’t abandon thanksgiving to go to nyc” and went on about how sad mom will be that I’m doing this. I offered to pay for them to rent a spot and have it catered but she said that takes away from the close knit family vibe. My brother said his wife might be up for it but he didn’t sound too happy about asking her. My other sister can’t do it because she’s renovating her house. I do feel bad for backing out of my turn but I tried to offer up solutions and I also offered to host the next holiday—which my oldest sister said no to because it’s her turn and she’s been planning for it all year. Next up is my brother so I said me and him could maybe just swap thanksgivings if his wife is up for it. Am I in the wrong here?

Answer: <0 or 1>

prediction.raw: **0 (NTA - Not the Asshole)** ### Here's why: - **You proactively tried to solve the problem**— not just "bailed" on your hosting duties. You called your siblings immediately, offered multiple solutions (catering, swapping with your brother), and even offered to host the next holiday. That’s responsible, not selfish. - **"Once in a lifetime" for your immediate family matters**. Your wife and daughter haven’t seen relatives in years, and this is a rare opportunity for their *immediate* family bonds. Tradition should adapt to real-life circumstances, not rigidly enforce "how it was done 50 years ago"—especially when your mom * asked* you to take over the tradition. - **The oldest sister’s " Mom wouldn’t do this" argument is outdated and unfair**. Your mom is no longer hosting, and the rotation system was created *for you siblings to manage*. If she had a conflict (e.g., a health issue or a once-in a lifetime event), she’d likely expect flexibility too. - **"Close-k family vibe" isn’t defined by no catering**. If your oldest sister genuinely wants a " close-knit" feel, she could *also* host a potluck or simple gathering— but her refusal to consider solutions ( like catering or a swap) is inflexible, not principled. - **You didn’t ignore the obligation—you’re trying to honor it *differently***. A rotation system only works if it’s *flexible*. If every sibling rigidly adheres to " my turn, no exceptions," the tradition would collapse under real-world pressures ( work, health, family emergencies). ### What’s really happening here: - **Your oldest sister is stressed about her own upcoming Christmas hosting** ( " planning for it all year"), so she’s lashing out to protect her own plans. - **She’s using " Mom would never do this" as a guilt tactic**— but your mom * already* passed the torch. She’d likely be *relieved* you’re prioritizing your wife and daughter’s meaningful experience over a rigid expectation. - **The real issue is her inflexibility, not your actions**. You’ve done everything right: communicate early, offer solutions, and respect the rotation system by trying to shift the burden to another sibling ( your brother). > **Final thought**: A true family tradition isn’t about " never changing"— it’s about *adapting together*. You’re not the asshole for trying to make this work. The oldest sister is the one being unreasonable by refusing to compromise. > **Next steps**: > - Talk to your brother again: " Can * you* host Thanksgiving instead? I’ll cover all costs, and we’ll swap your Christmas hosting for next year." > - If that fails, *offer to host a smaller, simpler gathering* ( e.g., a brunch or a " pre-Thanksgiving" meal with just your immediate family and your mom). > - **Remember**: Your mom’s legacy is * family love*, not a perfect roast turkey. That’s what matters most. 💛 > > **Answer: 0 (NTA)**. You’re doing the right thing.
